Topic.label: Basic Straightedge and Compass Constructions: Copying an Angle and Constructing an Angle Bisector

Question: To construct the bisector of \(\angle AOB\) using a straightedge and compass, first draw an arc centered at \(O\) that meets \(OA\) and \(OB\) at \(C\) and \(D\). Then draw arcs with the same radius centered at \(C\) and \(D\), meeting at \(P\) inside the angle. To ensure that the two arcs intersect, this radius must be:
Solution:
Assume the usual construction of an angle with \(0<\angle AOB<180^\circ\). Let \(d=CD>0\), and let \(r>0\) be the common radius of the two arcs. Any common point \(P\) must satisfy
\[
d\le CP+PD=2r,
\]
so \(r\ge d/2\). If the arcs are required to cross, \(C,D,P\) form a nondegenerate triangle, making the inequality strict. The side lengths \(r,r,d\) form such a triangle when \(2r>d\), so the crossing-arcs convention gives \(r>CD/2\), choice C. The radius is not required to equal \(CD\).

The equality case also matters because the question only says the arcs meet. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(CD\). It lies inside the angle. When \(r=d/2\), the circles are tangent at \(M\), since \(CM=DM=r\). Moreover,
\[
OC=OD,\qquad CM=DM,\qquad OM=OM.
\]
Thus \(\triangle OCM\cong\triangle ODM\) by SSS, giving \(\angle COM=\angle DOM\). Therefore \(OM\) is a valid angle bisector even with the radius in B.

For \(r<d/2\), the arcs cannot meet because \(2r<d\). Hence meeting allows \(r\ge CD/2\), while crossing requires \(r>CD/2\). The intended key C assumes crossing; it must not be enforced exclusively under the displayed wording.
